newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuela banks feel the heat as key auction nears.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela banks feel the heat as key auction nears.

text.p: The heat is suddenly rising for Venezuela's banks: if all goes as it should, three of the country's largest will be foreign-owned by January.
"Think of it! Competition by the new players will force the rest of the field to modernize or drop out," ran an editorial in financial weekly VenEconomy.

Such a scenario would have been almost unimaginable only a year ago. But barring any unforeseen last-minute glitches, the country's second and fourth largest banks -- Banco de Venezuela and Banco Consolidado -- will be auctioned on Thursday by national State Deposits Guarantee Fund Fogade.
More is at stake than their respective base auction prices of $286 million and $148 million, analysts say.
A successful sale will be taken as an auspicious sign for the government's privatization program.
The entry of well-capitalized, reputable foreign buyers will also mark a sea change in a sector still weak after a 1994-5 financial crisis absorbed some $11 billion in state bail-outs.
"With the privatization of these banks we will be able to say an important part of the financial crisis is over," Fogade president Esther de Margulis said late Tuesday.

Spain's Banco Santander and Colombia's Banco de Bogota are widely tipped as successful bidders. Spanish bank Banco Bilbao de Vizcaya is also reportedly set to take a leading share in Venezuela's largest bank, Banco Provincial after Credit Lyonnais was ordered by the the European Union to sell its 16 percent share.
"If I was one of Venezuela's other banks I'd be very alarmed," said one New York-based investor who closely tracks Venezuela. "The potential buyers are massive banks."
The aggressive and technologically advanced foreigners will look to take advantage of virgin banking territory, analysts say.
"Venezuelan retail banks have sat on their laurels for too long. The market here is totally undeveloped," said local InvestAnalysis consultant Alex Dalmady.
"Mortgage financing does not exist, and two thirds of all cars are still bought for cash," he added.
Among the first to feel the heat will be the country's third largest bank, Banco Mercantil.

"The question is: how will Mercantil survive? By itself, or will it need a foreign partner?" noted the New York investor. Only last week Mercantil president Gustavo Maturet denied rumors that shareholders were negotiating a sell-out to Banco Santander.
Most surprising is the speed at which the sector appears be re-organizing itself out ahead of the sale, analysts say.
"Everyone's been talking of the need for consolidation for a long time," said the investor. "Only now it seems to be happening, faster than anyone expected and via market forces."

Many of the largest banks are converting to universal banks in order to trim costs and boost efficiency. But despite the promising signs, neither the sales nor the sector's shake-out are done deals -- yet.
An earlier attempt to auction Banco de Venezuela folded in August when the auction was torpedoed by a murky mix of banking and political interests.

This time, in an attempt to similar quash nationalistic calls, the government has sold 10 percent of Banco de Venezuela and six percent of Banco Consolidado to local investors in a widely advertised popular share offering.

Legal claims, although rejected by the Supreme Court in October, are also pending against Banco de Venezuela and Consolidado by former owner Alvaro Stelling who argues he was cheated when forced to sell the banks to the state for one bolivar each when they folded in 1994.
Even if the auctions take place analysts say it is notoriously hard for foreigners to succeed at retail banking.
"The Spaniards may do better than most, but while the local banks are famously inefficient they do know their way around the market. That's an important plus," said the investor.
Analysts say the foreign banks may also find it hard to steer through the maze of relationships and favors that link many Venezuelan banks with the country's two main political parties.
((-- Caracas newsroom, 582 505 2600))
